Cons:

* The bomb defusal mission is just nonsensical. While it's obviously designed and written to be deliberately confusing to challenge the player, it is also ridiculous. The supervisor, Skinner, would be handling this, or at least offering assistance, not just casually leaving another agent's life up to a 3rd day employee who is reading the bomb defusal manual for the first time. Was having a good time in the game up until this mission. If you look at this achievement as well, only some ~50% of players have this achievement, and then you have to wonder, of those 50% how many had to look up a walk-through online in order to complete it? 
* Game was definitely somewhat dry at times where I felt a little bit bored. 
* I won't spoil any specifics but I will say the ending of the game is...not good, in my opinion. 

Pros:

* UI is clean and easy to use. The applications work smoothly without any issues. 
* Gameplay is straight forward and easy to understand. 
* Solid voice acting. 
* Storytelling is pretty engaging. 
* Game very stable, zero crashes or bugs / glitches. 
* No additional DRM beyond Steam.
* No Epic Online Services.

Gameplay Style: Point and click with some typing here and there related to puzzle solving. This requires some research into files on your in-game computer as well as using the provided tools as well. 

Game Length: ~5 Hours or thereabouts. 

Final Rating: 4.5/10. I got the game on sale and puzzle games aren't usually my thing but I wanted to give it a try as it sounded interesting and I like to support indie developers when I can, but this is a game that, despite some story aspects being well-done, the ending soured things for me as well as the bomb defusal mission to the point that I really would not recommend the game to others.

review_text_raw:
Some interesting concepts and a fun story. Cool twist too. Most of the puzzles were relatively straightforward, but the "manual reading" one was actually pretty exciting and interesting, and the "identifying the feed" one was clever. I just could not get past the ridiculous anachronisms popping up constantly, and some very confusing internal logic.

This game takes place in 1992. Everybody has a cell phone, digital photography is commonly accessible, "zoom, enhance" is an actual mechanic. The game's FBI analogue has a database with facial recognition data of nearly everyone in the country? In 1992??? In 2025 sure, but not in 1992. Agents are constantly uploading files to your computer from their phone. At one point, confusingly, an agent apparently sends you physical floppy disks.... via his phone...? Baffling honestly. I was willing to set aside the fact that VoIP didn't exist in 1992 either, but after a while you simply cannot suspend your disbelief any further. 

HAL's "hacking" capabilities are completely inconsistent, and the justifications for why they can't hack a particular thing make no narrative sense a lot of the time. Credit where credit's due though, nothing stands out to me as anachronistic about HAL's methods at least.

There's a big narrative-UX disconnect as well. Initially I thought the "phone calls" you receive from agents are just game objects showing transcripts of audio conversations, but at one point you're instructed to *enter a code into the chat box* as though it were a terminal. So now I'm asked to believe that my computer has been *actually transcribing* phone calls automatically while people are speaking to me, and that I can use this function as a terminal. Completely ridiculous. 

This game would have made way more sense if it were set in the current year, with minimal changes to the story or mechanics, but I think the devs were just too enamoured with the retro aesthetic to let it go so they set it in the 90s anyways. 

Side note: I had annoying bug where my keybinds weren't showing up in-game, so anything where I was required to press a key just had [???] instead. Not game breaking, just annoying.

I wish I liked this more. This is not a game about being an FBI operator, solving cases with little guidance. This is a standard conspiracy game that pretends to have options when it is all very railroaded. The game is:
5% cool deductive work, 
70% listening to people re-explain what is happening in case you quit and reloaded the game after each day
25% watching a black screen and listening to someone walking home

I like the controls, as simple as they are. But I am shocked to see people compare this to anything like Obra Dinn or Case of the Golden Idol. If you have are ok with a corny story, lots of reading and listening (not detective work, just fluff), and one of the worst time-sensitive, feel-bad, mini games if seen in a game like this, then you might actually enjoy your time. This is a $5 game on sale if you have exhausted the other detective games on Steam.

review_text_raw:
"The Operator" is a good game, except it isn't actually a game... It is more of an interactive film, where your choice doesn't actually matter, for example, despite several attempts to play for the agency, I couldn't do so, you always have to side with some renegade hacker("HAL"). The game just locks in dialogue options, so you can only comply to progress further in the game. When she reveals her identity, you can't report her, which proves how choice doesn't matter in this game, even the dialogue options aren't that much of a choice, as the respondents largely react similarly. Also, many actions in it don't have consequences, like you can mess up all the tasks hundreds of times, and the game just tells you you are wrong, not the characters, the game, like, you can (in some cases) just blindly click the screen and eventually you will get it right. Or with how you can mess up the bomb diffusal and subsequently kill a federal agent, with no consequences. 
Generally, the game is well made, and I have not found any bugs, but the crippling lack of player agency, and no consequences for wrong choices just make the game unplayable, and I would, therefore, not recommend it to other people, as a game at least. As I said, this isn't a game it is an interactive activity, that uses the mechanics of a game.

The game is extremely short and the puzzles are pretty much on guide rails and don't take much effort. The only difficult puzzle was the bomb but only due to the manual not making much sense. The entire game took me just under 4 hours but at least 30 minutes of that was somewhat needless transition footage that I wanted to skip and had almost zero impact on the game.

I had the twist figured out half way through the game and the ending was pretty obvious. I got the game on sale for $10.49 and justify it to myself that a movie ticket probably costs more these days. I was highly disappointed in the very small bit of content and how easy the puzzles were. The production wasn't bad, the concept wasn't bad, and there weren't any bugs I ran into so if there were an option between yes and no for recommendations I would choose that.

review_text_raw:
The game has potential but it is way overpriced for how long it takes. Will take 5 hours tops if you take your time to get all of the achievements. Also unfortunately it seems like the game is very linear, there are a few decisions you can make but I doubt they would change much to the ending. Also, there is a plot twist that is supposed to be a huge reveal and that I unfortunately saw coming a mile away, and I think most people would too.

Also, there is a terminal in the game, which is a neat touch, but it has some bugs (some commands that are listed in help don't work like they should) and it is never used besides typing commands that you are told to type. I was initially very excited about it but ended up disappointed that it doesn't have much use.

** Spoilers below **

For example, at some point you are given a command to call someone by typing their IP in the terminal, so I started writing down everyone's IP since I thought it would be useful later and I would be able to call them, but no. 99% of the notes I took in the notepad ended up being useless because the game's story lacks depth.
